note: Existing-source, strict-license-screened public gallery. Additional historical photos remain held from this site. Anatomy overlays are teaching annotations, not a separate verified voucher determination.

tiles.heading: 01 · LOOK HERE FIRST — SHORT, APPRESSED RED-GRAMA BRANCHES
tiles.details: Published ranges place flowering culms around 10–40 cm and individual branches around 12–25 mm. Existing species panels 1–3 show thin, often reddish ascending-to-appressed branches; color is variable and cannot establish the species. Count branches on a single attached flowering stem rather than across overlapping stems.
tiles.short: Follow ONE wiry perennial flowering culm: usually 2–7 slender one-sided branches hugging the axis.
tiles.status: REAL BRANCH ARCHITECTURE — CONNECTED RULER-SCALED CULM NEEDED

tiles.heading: 02 · LOW PERENNIAL TUFT AND TRUE HAIR LIGULE
tiles.details: The measured source describes blades commonly about 1–1.5 mm wide and occasional short rhizomes. Examine a blade–sheath junction from the SAME flowering plant to see the true ligule hairs rather than hairs on the sheath edge. No defensible species-specific ligule length in millimeters is established in the current evidence; do not invent one or arrow an unresolved fringe.
tiles.short: Small tufted perennial with narrow basal blades; true ligule is a short HAIR FRINGE.
tiles.status: SOURCE-BASED GROWTH FORM — CALIBRATED TRUE LIGULE MISSING

tiles.heading: 03 · MEASURE ONE COMPLETE FLOWERING BRANCH
tiles.details: Use an intact attached branch and millimeter scale. Mature spikelets are about 4–5 mm long, excluding projecting awns; count spikelets on one branch. Existing close photographs show branch shape but do not establish exact counts or glume lengths. Never measure a long awn as part of the spikelet body.
tiles.short: Each 12–25 mm one-sided branch often carries 8–24(–32) crowded spikelets.
tiles.status: REAL BRANCH PHOTOS — MATURE CALIBRATED SPIKELET GAP

tiles.heading: 04 · TWO GLUMES AND THREE FERTILE-LEMMA AWNS
tiles.details: The paired one-veined glumes persist below a basal fertile floret and a diminished upper floret. A mature fertile lemma is three-veined and deeply three-lobed, bearing THREE awns typically ~3–4 mm in Kew's treatment; the reduced upper floret may ALSO bear awns. Separate both florets under 10–20× before assigning any awn to the fertile lemma. Awn count and exact origin are NOT pixel-verified in the existing wide photographs.
tiles.short: Spikelet ~4–5 mm; lower glume ~3–4 mm, upper ~4–5 mm; fertile lemma body ~2 mm.
tiles.status: PUBLISHED DISSECTION CHARACTERS — NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO AND NO MICRO ARROWS

tiles.heading: 05 · CENTRAL TEXAS LOOK-ALIKES
tiles.details: Comparison panel 6 is Bouteloua rigidiseta (Texas grama), NOT red grama. Hairy grama B. hirsuta and B. pectinata usually show broader combs; blue grama B. gracilis has curved eyebrow-like combs. The thin, reddish branches are only a first clue: confirm glumes and the three fertile-lemma awns to separate overlapping mature material. Avoid forcing species ID from red color.
tiles.short: Texas grama has short fuzzy clusters; hairy grama has broader combs and a bare tip stinger.
tiles.status: REAL LOOK-ALIKE COMPARISON — MATCHED MATURE ANATOMY MISSING

tiles.heading: 06 · PUBLIC-READY GATE / TWO HANDOFFS
tiles.details: NEEDS_PUBLIC_PHOTO (Grass Photo-Finish): voucher-linked rooted Central Texas perennial and full 10–40 cm flowering culm; 12–25 mm attached branch and mature ~4–5 mm spikelets with 1-mm scale; both glumes, fertile three-awned lemma and separate reduced upper floret dissected at 10–20×; true hair-fringe ligule with 0.5-mm reference; same-scale Texas/hairy grama comparisons. NEEDS_SITE_QA (Public Learner Readiness): verify five locally archived images plus two external reference records, source IDs and per-image CC BY/CC BY-NC/public-domain terms, existing arrows, other-species panel labels, six-tile mobile layout and public page. Do not mark FINISHED or claim newly verified photos or arrows.
tiles.short: FIELD_READY_PHOTO_GAPS: seven retained photo records, but ligule and three-awn origins remain unproven.

steps.title: 1 · First, recognize the plant
steps.look_for: A small WIRY grama with thin branching stems and typically TWO TO SEVEN narrow branches that lie quite close to the axis (APPRESSED). Many flowering parts are red to purplish, but do not rely on color. On a magnified spikelet inspect the three awns that give 'threeawn grama' its name; the awn count is not proven from the distant photos.
steps.why_it_matters: Start with the recorded recognition characters before making a species identification.

steps.title: 2 · Examine the whole plant
steps.look_for: Use the finger-scale field macro to find the thin greenish flowering axis and the long skinny appressed reddish branchlets, not broad eyebrow combs.
steps.why_it_matters: Habit and growing context are supporting evidence, not proof of hidden roots or rhizomes.

steps.title: 3 · Inspect leaves, collar and nodes
steps.look_for: The measured source describes blades commonly about 1–1.5 mm wide and occasional short rhizomes. Examine a blade–sheath junction from the SAME flowering plant to see the true ligule hairs rather than hairs on the sheath edge. No defensible species-specific ligule length in millimeters is established in the current evidence; do not invent one or arrow an unresolved fringe.
steps.why_it_matters: Examine the real structures; the photo may not expose or measure all the described characters.

steps.title: 4 · Check the flowering structure
steps.look_for: Use an intact attached branch and millimeter scale. Mature spikelets are about 4–5 mm long, excluding projecting awns; count spikelets on one branch. Existing close photographs show branch shape but do not establish exact counts or glume lengths. Never measure a long awn as part of the spikelet body.
steps.why_it_matters: Use an attached, correctly identified specimen when deciding the flower or spikelet structures.

steps.title: 5 · Compare similar grasses
steps.look_for: Red grama's narrow reddish APPRESSED units on very fine wiry culms contrast with Texas grama's short clustered woolly/awned branches, hairy grama's broader stinger-bearing combs, and pectinata's robust long combs. Thin branches alone do not establish the species; a close mature three-awned spikelet is needed.
steps.why_it_matters: Confirm at least two independent botanical characters; do not remove a native candidate from color alone.
